speaker: maya
text: Last time: one 22-year-old's shot in the rain, a war gone global, and London sending the bill. This time: no new material. Eight episodes, ten questions, 1607 to 1763, in about thirteen and a half minutes. Jay's holding the list. The dare: say every answer out loud before I do. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now.

speaker: jay
text: Question one. Four empires, one continent. Match the model, one breath each.

speaker: maya
text: Spain: crown-run, souls and silver. Missions to convert, mines to pay, the crown skimming its fifth off the silver, and the casta labels ranking your grandparents.

speaker: jay
text: Souls paid for by silver.

speaker: maya
text: France: a fur empire. Beaver pelts for felt hats, Champlain's Quebec in 1608, and the colony stayed thin because a fur economy needed no farmers. The coureurs de bois paddled past the legal trading posts, and the crown barred the Huguenots, so the settlers never came.

speaker: jay
text: Thin by design, almost.

speaker: maya
text: Holland: a company colony. 1629: ship fifty settlers across and the company hands you a patroon estate, sixteen miles of riverfront on both banks. No wait — sixteen one side, eight both sides. Rensselaerswijck worked; most of the other patroons couldn't find tenants. But New Amsterdam did: a jumble of languages on the docks, a Dutch governor who couldn't shut the doors, and an English fleet taking it all in 1664.

speaker: jay
text: And England?

speaker: maya
text: Company money, settler families, farms. The headright paid fifty acres to whoever paid your passage: the planter, not the servant. And the Native answer, all four at once: Spain folded Native peoples into its labor machine, France allied with the Wendat against the Iroquois, Holland traded, and England pushed them off the land.

speaker: jay
text: Question two. Servants to slaves: walk the chain.

speaker: maya
text: Start with the deal: four to seven years of labor for a boat ticket. Finish and collect freedom dues: a little corn, some clothes, maybe land. Then the system worked too well: the servants lived, and wanted land that was already taken.

speaker: jay
text: And Berkeley crushed the rebellion, right? He won.

speaker: maya
text: He won the battle and lost the job. Bacon raised four to five hundred men in 1676, attacked even the Pamunkeys, English allies, burned Jamestown in September, and died of dysentery the next month. Berkeley hanged twenty-three of the leaders, and London recalled him anyway. The planters' lesson: never let the poor unite across race again.

speaker: jay
text: So they rebuilt the workforce on race.

speaker: maya
text: Piece by piece, and the supply helped: the Dutch monopoly broke in 1682, so enslaved Africans got cheaper just as servants got scarcer. 1640: three runaways caught, two white, one Black. The white men got four more years; John Punch got life. 1662: a child's status followed the mother, so slavery became hereditary. Barbados wrote the template in 1661, Carolina's planters carried it north, and Virginia's 1705 code gathered decades of law into one book: slavery for life, people held as real estate.

speaker: jay
text: Don't write that 1705 started it.

speaker: maya
text: The code gathered; it didn't invent. And the historians' fight rides with it: did the racism make the slavery, or the slavery make the racism? Both sides have evidence. The codes are the fact; the motive is the argument.

speaker: jay
text: Question three. New England: why'd they come, and who got kicked off the hill?

speaker: jay
text: The Pilgrims and the Puritans, same people, right? Funny hats, Thanksgiving?

speaker: maya
text: Different group, different decade. Plymouth's Pilgrims, 1620: Separatists, breaking with the Church of England for good. Massachusetts Bay, 1630: Puritans, still trying to purify it from within. More than twenty thousand crossed by 1640, and they came as families, not fortune-hunters. They crossed for their own religion, not everyone's. And the hill kicked people off it. Roger Williams, banished in 1635 for saying the colony had no right to Native land it hadn't bought. Anne Hutchinson, tried in 1637 for preaching against the ministers, excommunicated and gone by 1638.

speaker: jay
text: And the towns ran on covenant.

speaker: maya
text: Church and town fused into one contract with God, the meetinghouse at the center. Then the war: King Philip's War, 1675 to '76. Metacom, Massasoit's son. The spark was an English court hanging three of his men. Seventeen settlements destroyed, fifty more damaged. And say the per-capita part, or the deadliest label is wrong. The book everyone read afterward: Rowlandson's captivity narrative, 1682. Some call it America's first bestseller. Native power in New England never really came back.

speaker: jay
text: Question four. The middle colonies: the diversity lab.

speaker: maya
text: Penn's Holy Experiment, 1681: a colony paid for a debt, advertised in German, because empty land pays nothing. The Pennsylvania Dutch: Deutsch, not Dutch. Palatine Germans, roughly a third of the colony by the Revolution, and something like half of them arrived as redemptioners: negotiating their servitude on the dock, sick and broke, instead of back in Europe.

speaker: jay
text: And the Scots-Irish on the frontier.

speaker: maya
text: Ulster Presbyterians, roughly a fourth of the colony, pushed west onto the frontier. Wheat and corn, the breadbasket, flour sailing south to feed the sugar islands. Franklin's 1751 essay fretted the Germans would Germanize Pennsylvania instead of Pennsylvania Anglicizing them, which tells you how German it had gotten.

speaker: jay
text: So Quakers, no slaves. That was the brand.

speaker: maya
text: The brand, not the books. Penn himself held enslaved people. In 1688 four German Quakers signed the first protest against slavery in the English colonies, and the Yearly Meeting filed it away. Then 1737: Penn's sons turned a day-and-a-half deed into a footrace and walked off with a Rhode Island-sized piece of Lenape land. Pluralist, not necessarily tolerant.

speaker: jay
text: Question five. Mercantilism: the theory, the rules, the dodge.

speaker: maya
text: The theory: the world's wealth is a fixed pile, and power is how much of it sits in your vaults. The colonies ship raw materials cheap, buy finished goods dear, and never build the factory. Some historians call that a decent bargain: protected markets, the Navy's guarded sea lanes. Others call it a cage.

speaker: jay
text: The rules had names and dates.

speaker: maya
text: 1651, aimed at the Dutch: trade on English ships. 1660: the enumerated list, tobacco leading it, to England only. 1663: European goods pass through an English port first. The list kept growing: rice, then naval stores, and Parliament fenced off the factories: Wool in 1699, Hat in 1732, Iron in 1750.

speaker: jay
text: And every ship sailed the triangle, all three legs.

speaker: maya
text: Pattern, not the average voyage. Plenty of ships ran two legs and never closed the loop. New England rum sailed straight to the Caribbean. The arrows simplified the voyages; the chain didn't lie: distilleries needed Caribbean sugar, sugar plantations needed enslaved labor.

speaker: jay
text: The dodge worked because nobody enforced the rules.

speaker: maya
text: Salutary neglect. Walpole's supposed line was "let sleeping dogs lie." Supposed, because nobody's fully sure he said those words. But the neglect was real: understaffed customs, governors looking away, 1721 to 1742. Burke finally gave it the name in 1775, looking back at commerce grown something like twelvefold since 1700. And the poster boy: Hancock's Liberty, seized in 1768 on smuggling charges that were dropped for lack of evidence. Charged; never convicted.

speaker: jay
text: My grandmother still points at the dotted line on my birthday cards and says "put your John Hancock here."

speaker: maya
text: She means the signature. The fortune came first, and some of it came through the back door.

speaker: jay
text: Question six. The Awakening: heart, head, and the split.

speaker: jay
text: Whitefield started the whole thing, right? The fields, the crowds?

speaker: maya
text: The trap answer. The fire was smoldering in the 1730s: cold churches, the halfway compromise of 1662. Whitefield poured the gasoline: 1739, mid-twenties, open fields, crowds in the thousands, newspapers claiming twenty-five thousand. Franklin walked backward down Market Street doing the math and computed thirty thousand could hear him.

speaker: jay
text: And Edwards was the loud one.

speaker: maya
text: Backwards. Whitefield's the act: the weeping, the crowds. Edwards read his sermon nearly flat, the famous account says barely looking up, while the room came apart. Enfield, July 1741, the spider over the fire: his actual words. His own congregation voted him out in 1750 anyway.

speaker: jay
text: While Franklin was indoors reasoning.

speaker: maya
text: The counterweight. Poor Richard's Almanack from 1732, the Junto debating club from 1727, and deism: God wound the clock and stepped back. The kite story's shakier than the textbooks say, but the lightning work was real. Then the split: New Lights for the revival, Old Lights for the old guard, though I always want to flip those, and the organizing taught ordinary colonists to defy authority and survive it.

speaker: jay
text: Which is why some historians say it rehearsed the Revolution.

speaker: maya
text: Some say rehearsal; others say the fires burned out decades before 1776. Argue both sides.

speaker: jay
text: Question seven. How'd the assemblies get powerful while London looked away?

speaker: jay
text: The purse.

speaker: maya
text: The purse. They voted the taxes, the budget, and in a lot of colonies the governor's own salary. Massachusetts proved it in the 1720s: Shute demanded a permanent salary, the House voted his pay year by year instead. Burnet tried next; in 1728 they handed him seventeen hundred pounds and still refused the fixed salary.

speaker: jay
text: And the Zenger verdict fixed press law for good.

speaker: maya
text: The trap, not the truth. Cosby jailed printer Zenger in 1734, after the paper printed his sacking of a judge over a salary dispute. Zenger sat in jail the better part of a year; his wife Anna kept the paper printing. Hamilton argued truth should be the defense; the judge barred it. The jury acquitted anyway. The law on the books stayed ugly; the idea changed.

speaker: jay
text: And Anglicization means they were becoming American.

speaker: maya
text: The reverse. They were getting more British, not more American. English tea, English newspapers, English wigs, and the more British they felt, the harder they insisted on Englishmen's rights: assemblies, trials, presses. Their Britishness was the weapon.

speaker: jay
text: Question eight. The war: one shot, one plan, one gamble.

speaker: maya
text: May 1754, Jumonville Glen, before dawn, in the rain. Washington, twenty-two, about forty men around a French camp. Somebody fires; the French commander dies. France called it murder, and the man was an ensign, a junior officer, not a general. Washington signed the surrender paper at Fort Necessity in French he couldn't read, and the French word in it was l'assassinat. Assassination. They carried it home like a confession.

speaker: jay
text: The shot heard 'round the world.

speaker: maya
text: Different shot. Emerson's poem. Lexington and Concord, 1775. This one started a world war and nobody wrote a poem about it.

speaker: jay
text: Then the Albany Plan united the colonies.

speaker: maya
text: The colonies said no first. They weren't disorganized; they were guarding their own power. Then London said no too. Then Braddock: July 1755, nearly fifteen hundred regulars marching on Fort Duquesne, and a smaller French and Native force shot them to pieces from the tree line at the Monongahela. European lines in American woods. Washington rode out with four bullets through his coat: his actual words, from his July 1755 letter home.

speaker: jay
text: And Pitt's gamble won it.

speaker: maya
text: 1757. Spend in North America, pin France in Europe: "conquer America in Germany," the line attributed to him. Quebec, September 1759: under an hour, both generals dead. The Treaty of Paris, February 1763: Canada and everything east of the Mississippi to Britain. France kept the sugar islands, Guadeloupe and Martinique. A continent traded for sugar.

speaker: jay
text: Question nine. 1763: why did winning break everything?

speaker: maya
text: The bill. An enormous debt. The books won't pin the number, and neither will I. Pontiac's rising the moment the French left: the British had ended the gift diplomacy, and his warriors besieged Detroit while forts fell across the lakes. Hundreds of soldiers, thousands of colonists, more than a year to break it.

speaker: jay
text: So London punished the colonists with the Proclamation.

speaker: maya
text: Follow the money, not the revenge. October 1763: no settlement west of the Appalachians, because London wanted the frontier wars off its books. The colonists walked over the line anyway, including Washington, whose bounty land for his Virginia Regiment froze under it. And the century of looking the other way? Over.

speaker: jay
text: Last one. Question ten: the whole unit, one sentence.

speaker: jay
text: Growth made the colonies too valuable, too diverse, and too used to running themselves to be ruled on London's old terms. When London tried anyway, the arrangement broke.

speaker: maya
text: The period thesis. Keep it. Eight episodes, ten questions. Land them in one breath. Four empires, four hungers, and the Native peoples folded, allied, traded with, and pushed aside. Servants to slaves: the rebellion taught the planters to divide by race, and the 1705 codes: did they start it, or gather it? Gathered. The codes gathered decades of law. Covenant towns that banished their dissenters, then broke in King Philip's War. Penn's experiment: many peoples, unequal footing. Mercantilism's fixed pile, the Acts, the dodge, the neglect. The Awakening's heart and Franklin's head. The purse, the press, and the Britishness. One shot in the rain, Pitt's gamble, and a bill London couldn't pay without the colonies.

speaker: maya
text: Two predictions I'd bet on. One: evaluate the extent to which the British colonies had developed a distinct identity and self-government by 1754. Your turn.

speaker: maya
text: Extensive self-government, thin distinct identity. The assemblies held the purse, a colonial jury acquitted Zenger, and decades of salutary neglect trained the colonies to rule themselves, yet Anglicization had them drinking English tea and demanding Englishmen's rights. The complexity point: the machinery was American, the loyalty was British, and the war starting in 1754 would test which one held.

speaker: maya
text: Two: evaluate the extent to which the shift from indentured servitude to enslaved labor transformed the Chesapeake between 1660 and 1700. Your turn.

speaker: maya
text: The labor force transformed; the engine didn't. Term contracts became lifetime, hereditary, race-coded slavery, written down from John Punch in 1640 to Virginia's 1705 code. But tobacco still demanded land and workers, and the planters' hunger never changed. The transformation was legal and racial. The economy barely changed.

speaker: jay
text: Valuable, diverse, self-governing —

speaker: maya
text: and ungovernable on London's old terms.

speaker: jay
text: Next time: the tax bills come due, and the colonies push back.
